item.title: Uncertainty in the Verbalizable Workspace
item.description:
Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt.

TL;DR:

We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens. Its readout helps us spot answers that are more likely to be wrong. Surprisingly, just counting the tokens in a model’s reasoning gives us a good indicator of whether the final answer is right or wrong. Wrong answers tend to come with longer reasoning traces. To mitigate this potential shortcut, we also compared traces of similar length, and the U-lens holds its ground across three models and four benchmarks. Notably, our approach is label-free and requires just a single forward pass, while many other methods require training or multiple passes. The U-lens also held up in our out-of-domain analysis across benchmarks better than many trained probes. Finally, early tests on emotions and reward-hacking responses hint that similar readouts could help model harnesses flag suspicious behavior.
We’ve open-sourced the code.

Introduction

Birth of the idea

Earlier this year, Anthropic connected the global workspace theory to large language models (LLMs). They showed that a model’s hidden state includes concepts that are not necessarily verbalized in the output but nonetheless used during intermediate reasoning. Intrigued, we wanted to put this new form of semantic readout to work on something with direct real-world applications. Coincidentally, one of us had just stumbled upon a paper by Kumaran et al. that discusses a language model’s metacognitive awareness of its own uncertainty. The authors found that the output probabilities a model emits during the autoregressive generation of its answer and the self-reported uncertainty that it expresses when explicitly asked for it (e.g., “How certain are you about this answer?”) contain complementary but not fully overlapping signals of its confidence. So we wondered (a) can we combine these two types of uncertainty signals in one estimator, and (b) can we improve the capture of the self-reported uncertainty by leveraging the Jacobian readout introduced in the J-lens?

Contributions

  • We built the U-space from four kinds of uncertainty: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. The alignment of a model’s hidden state with these basis directions allows us to watch different forms of uncertainty come and go as the model reasons.
  • We paired the interpretable U-space readout with the average entropy of the model’s token probabilities to get a scalar uncertainty score, the U-lens. It combines the two uncertainty signals discussed in Kumaran et al.
  • Across three models and four benchmarks, the U-lens was better at separating right from wrong answers than 12 other methods we tested. It held up even when we compared reasoning traces of similar length to remove a potential length confound.
  • We pushed one model along the uncertainty directions and made it hesitate over simple questions in different ways. The directions appear to affect the model's behavior rather than just describe it.
  • We tried the same construction beyond uncertainty. In early tests, it read emotions in comments and distinguished reward-hacking responses from genuine ones.

Background

When an LLM is unsure, it rarely says so. It usually produces a plausible but hallucinated answer. This uncertainty is intrinsic to the model. It is the dispersion of the model’s predictive state for a given query, and uncertainty quantification (UQ) estimates it. The uncertainty signal can be read from the model’s output or from its internal computation. For example, we can look at the probability the model assigns to its answer tokens or at how spread out its next-token probabilities are. We can also ask the model multiple times and compare whether the sampled answers mean the same thing, or ask it how likely its own answer is to be true. That last option is tempting, because we can apply it to open- and closed-source models without any interventions in the computation, but self-reported confidence is often overconfident. It also asks the model to turn its internal uncertainty into a string of tokens, which could be a noisy transformation.

Another line of work looks at the internal states of a language model and tries to put what it finds into a form we humans can understand. In a transformer, layers pass information through a shared residual stream. The vector in that stream at a particular layer and token position is what we call a hidden state. Each block reads from the stream and adds its contribution back, until the final state is used to predict the next token. The linear representation hypothesis suggests that at least some concepts show up as directions in these hidden states. U-space makes this bet for uncertainty. If different kinds of doubt have distinct directions in the residual stream, we can look for them without asking the model to put them into words. Several approaches try to read these intermediate states before the model produces its final output distribution. The logit lens reads a state as if it were the final one, skipping the remaining layers and applying the unembedding matrix directly. The tuned lens learns an auxiliary linear map before applying that matrix. The J-lens gets its map from the model itself. Its Jacobian asks how a small change in an intermediate hidden state would affect the final state of the current and later tokens, after passing through the remaining layers. Averaged across many contexts, this lets us read out concepts the model could put into words even when it does not.

where is the hidden state at layer and token position is the final layer, and the expectation runs over prompts and over the current and all later positions . is the unembedding matrix and the gain of the final RMSNorm. The R-lens improves early-layer readouts by adjusting the backward pass to reduce accumulated errors.

These lenses show us what the model represents during its computation, but they do not provide a measure of its uncertainty. The J-lens does give each vocabulary token a direction in the residual stream, though, and this gives us a place to start. First, find words that express different forms of uncertainty, then derive corresponding directions in the residual stream, and finally check how much the hidden states align with these directions.

Constructing the U-space

Finding the right basis

Before building the U-space, we need to decide what kinds of uncertainty should build its basis directions. For the U-space, we want categories that make intuitive sense, have roots in the literature, and are few enough that we can still tell them apart cleanly. We compare several candidates. The aleatoric and epistemic split separates model-independent randomness from a lack of knowledge of the underlying input-output relationship. Klir and Wierman distinguish fuzziness (where does “tall” begin?), nonspecificity (which of several possibilities is right?), and discord (what if the evidence disagrees?). Prince et al. distinguish four simple ways of softening a claim: making it less exact (“sort of”), making a number approximate (“about twenty”), signaling personal uncertainty (“I think”), or shifting responsibility to another source (“according to the report”). AmbigQA looks at ambiguity in questions: which event or entity is meant, what property or type of answer is sought, whether the answer depends on time, or whether several questions have been rolled into one. Finally, we test a taxonomy inspired by Parsons. It groups uncertainty into four forms: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. We compare it with the other candidates on how intuitive their categories are and whether they strike the right balance, namely, enough to distinguish useful kinds of uncertainty, but few enough that we can still separate their signals and visualize them in 3D. We also test quantitatively how well each taxonomy helps us spot wrong answers.

Considering all criteria, we settle on the four categories inspired by Parsons: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. The last category leaves room for uncertainty that was not captured by the others, such as an unreliable source.

Author note: We could also get anchor words from the model itself. With contrastive prompts, the J-lens can read out words associated with each category. We stuck with published word lists to avoid depending on carefully crafted prompts, although words extracted from the model improved uncertainty prediction in preliminary experiments.
See Appendix B for examples of such contrastive prompts.

From words to residual-stream directions

Having four categories is one thing. Finding them in a model’s hidden states is another. We start with published lists of uncertainty and certainty words. A lightweight sentence encoder sorts all uncertainty words into our four categories using short definitions of each category. For instance, the word “contradictory” is assigned to the conflicting evidence category, while “dubious” is assigned to general uncertainty (see Appendix C). Next, we pull each word back through the J-lens.

where

  • : a one-hot vector that picks out word in the vocabulary,
  • : the unembedding matrix as above,
  • : the gain of the final normalization layer (RMSNorm) as above,
  • : the J-lens Jacobian, which describes how the final hidden state responds to changes in the hidden state at layer averaged over generic prompts,
  • : the resulting direction for word in the hidden states of layer

This tells us which direction in a chosen layer’s residual stream would raise that word’s output score. The word is now a direction we can look for inside the model, rather than something we need to find in its written answer. For each category, we average all corresponding uncertainty-word directions and subtract the average of all certainty-word directions. This helps cancel out what the two groups have in common and gives us a direction pointing toward that specific kind of uncertainty.

where and are the uncertainty and certainty words of category and scales a vector to unit length. We then make the four directions perpendicular and equally long. Together, they span the U-space.

This symmetric (Löwdin) orthonormalization keeps each column of as close as possible to its category direction . This takes no examples of correct or incorrect answers, requires no training.



Reading uncertainty from the U-space

With the four basis directions in place, we can follow the model as it reasons. At each step, we project its hidden state onto the U-space. This gives us four numbers, one for each kind of uncertainty, which we can plot across the reasoning trace.

where is the hidden state of reasoning token at the readout layer, the columns are the four U-space directions, and is the signed alignment with category We keep signals from different categories from canceling each other out. If the state aligns with conflicting evidence but points away from ambiguity, the conflicting-evidence signal should still count. We achieve this using the elementwise softplus function:

where , is applied on each coordinate, and the gain is fixed by the number of categories. A negative alignment with any of the axes shrinks toward zero instead of subtracting from a positive one. is a single score that rises when the hidden state points toward one or more uncertainty directions within the U-space (positive combinations of those directions form a cone within the U-space) and represents the verbalizable uncertainty referred to at the beginning. To get a single readout for the whole reasoning trace, we look at the hidden state at the end-of-thinking marker. By then, the model has processed all its reasoning, and we have one consistent point to inspect, no matter how long it took to get there (this will become important in the “Evaluating the U-lens” section, where we show that many other methods get strongly influenced by the length of the reasoning trace). This concludes the extraction of the verbalizable uncertainty signal that we discussed at the beginning. While the model does not explicitly report its uncertainty through its generated tokens, the signal is extracted from its residual stream. As also discussed there, we pair this verbalizable readout with a distributional signal from the model’s next-token probabilities. At each reasoning step, we measure how spread out those probabilities are, then average over the trace, so longer reasoning does not automatically mean a higher score.

where is the probability the model assigns to token of its vocabulary at the reasoning step and is the length of the reasoning trace Multiplying that average by the U-space readout gives us the U-lens uncertainty score.

where is the position of the end-of-thinking marker. A higher signals an answer that is more likely to be wrong.

Author note: We multiply the two signals so the U-space readout can adjust predictive entropy without a fitted scale. A more carefully tuned combination might spot more wrong answers, but would usually need calibration examples, which we wanted to avoid.



Evaluating the U-lens

The U-lens gives us two things to examine: four uncertainty signals we can follow token by token, and an overall score we can later compare with whether an answer is right. We test it on three open-weight reasoning models: Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen3.5-27B, and Magistral-Small-2507. We fix the readout layer in advance at two-thirds of each model’s depth: layer 40 of 60, 42 of 64, and 27 of 40, respectively. This is a simple way to land in the range where the J-lens reads intermediate representations well, after the earliest layers but before the final layers become dominated by the output token. It also keeps us from picking a favorable layer separately for each model. We use released J-lenses for Gemma and Qwen. For Magistral, we estimate one from 100 unlabeled WikiText-103 prompts using the reference implementation. Before checking whether the score predicts wrong answers, let’s see how it reads the different uncertainties from a single response to the question: “Was Hamlet left-handed, and did he love Ophelia?”

At first, the verbalized answer and the U-lens agree. Shakespeare never specifies Hamlet’s handedness, and incompleteness lights up. Then the answer becomes much firmer: “Yes, Hamlet did genuinely love Ophelia.” The readout tells a less settled story. It briefly shifts toward ambiguity at the word “play,” then conflicting evidence takes a larger share and remains prominent as the answer mentions Hamlet’s cruelty. General uncertainty also lights up at the apostrophe in “father’s.” (The lens might be picking up a more local kind of uncertainty, perhaps about grammar, but we did not test this further.)
Another example can be found in Appendix D.

The Hamlet example shows what the readout picks up in one answer. Now, we move to the quantitative evaluation and test whether the U-lens also helps to flag potentially erroneous answers across an entire set of questions. We test this on 1,000 questions each from MMLU-Pro, Omni-MATH, SuperGPQA, and TriviaQA. They cover broad reasoning, Olympiad mathematics, graduate-level knowledge, and factual recall. We sample three responses per question from each model. AUROC and AUPRC tell us how well high uncertainty scores pick out wrong answers. AURC tells us how the error rate changes as we set aside answers flagged as uncertain. One important phenomenon when evaluating uncertainty estimators is that incorrect reasoning traces tend to be longer than correct ones. Indeed, across our four benchmark comparisons, the median length of incorrect traces is between 1.33 and 4.79 times that of correct traces, although their length distributions overlap considerably. This creates a potential confound. A method might appear effective at predicting errors simply because it assigns higher uncertainty scores to longer responses, rather than identifying uncertainty in the model’s reasoning. We therefore score each method twice. First, we evaluate all responses together, allowing reasoning length to contribute whatever signal it carries. Then we compare responses of similar length: we split each evaluation set into ten groups by token count, calculate the same metrics within each group, and take an average weighted by group size. Comparing the two scores shows how much of a method’s performance is tied to response length.

We compare the U-lens against a range of methods that use different strategies to extract uncertainty signal. Generation length simply counts the number of reasoning tokens and uses the total length to predict whether an answer is correct. MSP, Predictive Entropy, Maximum Entropy, Mean NLL, Self-Certainty, and DeepConf draw on the token probabilities during autoregressive generation. P(True) asks the model plainly to judge the certainty of its answer in a second pass, TokUR perturbs its weights across several passes, and Semantic Entropy and SentenceSAR compare multiple sampled answers. We also include Feature-Gaps, which learns a hidden-state direction from labeled examples.

Length alone is a remarkably strong baseline. At 68.6% AUROC, it nearly matches the supervised Feature-Gaps method at 68.8%. But when we compare answers of similar length, its score falls to 52.4% (close to random guessing). TokUR, the strongest baseline on unadjusted AUROC, loses 9.4 points. The U-lens moves from 71.1% to 69.2%, but still claims the highest length-controlled AUROC. This suggests it picks up more than just how many tokens the model emitted to answer the question.

The workspace signal and entropy help each other

The U-lens combines two signals. The first is the verbalizable workspace signal, which we called in the construction of the U-space, and which is read from the hidden state at the end of reasoning. The second is the distributional signal, which is measured by the average predictive entropy of the next-token distributions during reasoning. We now want to test whether they capture the same uncertainty signal, or whether each adds something the other misses. We compare each signal on its own and with their combination in the U-lens score.

The two signals help in different ways depending on the model. For Gemma, the workspace signal and predictive entropy work about equally well on their own. Qwen gets more from entropy, while Magistral gets considerably more from the workspace signal. Combining them works better than either one alone for all three models.

Do the directions affect generation?

Our approach thus far shows that U-space directions can be used to identify uncertainty-related information in hidden states and thereby predict incorrect reasoning. However, this does not tell us whether these representations actually influence the model’s behavior. To determine this, we perform activation steering experiments by modifying the model’s hidden states along individual uncertainty directions and observing how its generation changes. For a hidden state we apply . Here, is the direction corresponding to one uncertainty category, while controls the strength of the intervention relative to the hidden state’s norm. This makes intervention strengths more comparable across layers and positions. We conduct the experiments on Qwen3.5-27B, steering blocks 32–54 in two settings:

  • Prompt-level steering: We modify activations during the prefill phase with thinking disabled. Asking the question “What is 2 + 2?” allows us to observe how each uncertainty direction affects a response that should ideally require little interpretation or uncertainty.
  • Reasoning-level steering: We intervene during a 50-token window inside the thinking process, beginning after a fixed prefix that the model has already generated.

For the exemplary question “What is 2 + 2?” the model still generates “4” at moderate intervention strengths, yet it introduces peculiar reasoning detours. Ambiguity steering leads the model to question whether the prompt itself is valid, and steering conflicting evidence causes the model to recall literature references where “2 + 2 = 5.” When steering within the reasoning process, amplifying the ambiguity direction causes the model to introduce an additional step, namely “Review for Ambiguity: Is there any trick?” before concluding with the arithmetic problem.

These experiments show us that the U-space directions are not merely useful for reading hidden states and that intervening along them can also change the model’s subsequent behavior. The evidence at this stage is preliminary. For now, the results provide an initial check that complements the general U-space methodology. They do not establish that these four axes constitute distinct causal mechanisms of uncertainty.

Does this approach generalize to other domains?

The recipe behind U-space starts with contrasting words, so we tried it beyond uncertainty. On GoEmotions, we built directions for anger, sadness, fear, and general negative feeling using words such as “angry” and “calm.” All four picked up their target in human-labeled Reddit comments, even when the comments contained none of our chosen words.

The sadness direction, for example, could distinguish sadness from other negative emotions, suggesting it captures a more specific semantic property beyond mere negative sentiment. We also tried School of Reward Hacks, where each task comes with one response that does what was asked and another that exploits the stated scoring rule, for example, by stuffing in keywords. This time, we let the model suggest the anchor words from examples, then used those words to construct a semantic direction.

The resulting direction separates unseen responses and cheat methods across all three models. The hacked responses are primarily decoded as bizarre or fake rather than an intent to cheat, but this is a clear signal nevertheless. The way a model expresses a certain semantic property internally might not one-for-one align with how humans would.

Does U-lens hold up when the domain changes?

A trained uncertainty estimator might learn something specific to the questions it was trained on. We tested this by fitting five hidden-state uncertainty probes on labeled answers from one benchmark, then applying them unchanged to the other three. We repeated this across MMLU-Pro, Omni-MATH, SuperGPQA, and TriviaQA. The U-lens uses no correctness labels, so there was nothing to refit.

The scores are length-controlled AUROC × 100. For each model and trained method, we fit a probe on one benchmark and test it on the other three. We repeat this with each of the four benchmarks as the training set, giving us twelve transfers to average. The U-lens needs no benchmark-specific fitting, so we simply average its results across the four benchmarks. The trained probes often did well on their own benchmark and lost ground when the questions changed. Mass-mean was the most stable of them, but the U-lens still came out ahead of the strongest transferred probe for each model. The margin on Gemma is smaller than on the other models. Across these four benchmarks, the result suggests that our uncertainty directions are less tied to a particular set of questions.

Limitations

Our results suggest that U-space provides a useful and novel way to detect and interpret internal uncertainty, yet several limitations remain. Firstly, the uncertainty categories are not exhaustive. Our four categories were chosen for their interpretability, but they do not necessarily reflect how models organize uncertainty internally. Furthermore, the method depends on the quality of the underlying lens. U-space relies on the J-lens to map semantic concepts back into the residual stream, meaning its effectiveness is contingent on how accurately the lens represents them. This could limit applicability to models where the J-lens is less reliable, such as smaller models. Although preparing a lens can require estimating an average Jacobian, it is relatively inexpensive and a one-time procedure involving backward passes through a frozen model, so no parameter optimization or task-specific labels are needed. Related to this is the limitation that applying the U-lens requires access to internal model states. The method requires hooks during generation to extract the hidden states and token-level predictive distributions to calculate the workspace signal and predictive entropy. To extend this to closed-source models would depend on providers exposing the required internal information or implementing the method themselves. Finally, we have not evaluated the method adversarially, yet. Our experiments focus more closely on standard reasoning benchmarks rather than examples deliberately constructed to expose weaknesses. Consequently, we do not yet know how robust the method is to adversarial prompts or attempts to produce misleading uncertainty signals. We leave this as an interesting continuation of our work.

Where this leaves us

We began by asking whether a model’s next-token probabilities and its verbalizable uncertainty could tell us different things, and whether we could read the latter without asking for a self-report. Our results suggest yes on both counts. The U-lens combines a workspace readout with average predictive entropy of the reasoning trace, and each signal adds something that the other misses. Together, they beat every single one of the twelve baselines we tested. We kept the method deliberately simple, without fitting a scale on labeled examples or using handcrafted contrastive prompts for the anchor words, so there is room to tune it for particular uses. The same way of building directions also showed promise beyond uncertainty. Our emotion and reward-hacking results were encouraging.

Before we close, let us move from uncertainty quantification to a broader question about oversight, or in other words, the question of whether we could see signs that a model is heading toward a harmful action. We used the J-lens to find uncertainty in a model’s computation without asking it to say what it was unsure about. Could we look for signs of a harmful plan in the same way? If we abuse the global workspace analogy, we could venture to consider the verbalizable representations in a model’s residual stream as the model’s “thoughts” it considers before answering. This leads us to a slightly brazen question about our own thoughts. Can a human craft a sophisticated, harmful plan without ever thinking about its harmfulness? Probably. But you would imagine that it becomes harder to carry out. We wonder if something similar could hold for models. A model can learn to hide misbehavior in its written reasoning, but we suspect a misaligned plan may still leave traces in its verbalizable workspace. Checking that space across tokens and layers might make those traces harder to hide. Our U-space directions are linear, though, and recent work on concept manifolds shows that some concepts form curved structures that a single direction captures only in part. We think combining checks throughout the reasoning with ways to read such structures is a promising question for oversight. Consider this pothead hypothesis as food for thought, nothing we tested. We do not know whether a misaligned plan must pass through the verbalizable workspace, or whether a model could easily learn to route around these checks. But even a monitor that makes evasion just a little bit harder might buy us time to develop better oversight.

item.title: Neural networks are not already clean
item.description:
What would it take to get assurance that we have actually explained a neuron? Certainly, it would be a good sign if neuron activations looked like they had a consistent pattern, and a bad sign if they looked like a random jumble of unrelated concepts.

Nick Cammarata’s recent post makes an important and true observation: in the past, people have been too quick to write off neurons as polysemantic, but if you look harder, there is actually often a simple pattern behind the activating examples. This historically caused people to overestimate how much polysemanticity there is. This is a really good point and we should update on it. But it’s nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously anticipated.

What does it take to explain a neuron?

It’s unclear whether there even is a simple pattern that explains every neuron.[1] But even if there is a simple pattern that matches the activating examples of a neuron, that still doesn’t mean that the explanation is correct.[2] Suppose we look at the top activating examples of a neuron, and they are all sentences like “Fred the poodle zipped down the street on his bicycle. ‘Wow, I didn’t know a dog could ride a bicycle!’ I exclaimed.” Top activations can often give a misleading impression of how monosemantic a neurons is, so next we look at the top 20th percentile of activations, and we find the examples are now things like “John rode on his bicycle while his dog trailed behind”. And when we check the weakest activations, they’re often still about dogs, just without bicycles — “The dog sauntered lazily down the street.” Given this evidence, can we conclude that the neuron is monosemantic, and that its meaning is “dogs riding bicycles”?

I argue we cannot. There are a few reasons why the vibes of activating examples might heavily mislead us about how interpretable a neuron is. First, just because every example that activates the neuron fits the pattern, doesn’t necessarily mean that the other way around is true; perhaps not all examples that fit the pattern also activate the neuron. Perhaps your neuron actually only activates on dogs on bicycles on sunny days, but you never noticed that. This turned out to be a pretty big problem with the auto interp paper.[3] In practice, it’s very common for neurons that look like they activate on X to actually only activate on a very specific subset of X that is hard to characterize compactly. If you forced the neuron to always activate on X, it would degrade the model.

Second, there might actually be really important information in the activation magnitudes. It might matter crucially whether the neuron is strongly or weakly activating, and if you have a hard time predicting which activations should be strong or weak, you might be missing a big part of the explanation. My best guess from all the results I've seen is that ablating small neuron activations quite substantially degrades model performance, so I don’t think we get to ignore weak activations completely.[4]

Simulation scores tell us whether we explained a neuron

To be able to claim that we understand a neuron, it’s insufficient for things to look kinda nice. If you can’t simulate the neuron in a way that doesn’t degrade the model, you don’t really understand the neuron. This requires writing a rubric—”If there’s a dog literally on a bicycle, that’s a 4.5; if there’s a dog and a bicycle but no riding, that’s a 3.2”, and so on—and then comparing that rubric against inputs and substituting neuron values with the simulated values. If this process heavily degrades the model, then our explanation was wrong.

Nick’s post argues that simulation scores are bad because they are too demanding — they force you to explain lots of stuff that doesn’t actually matter. However, I think this is just a byproduct of the kinda terrible correlation-based simulation scores used by the original auto interp paper, and is fixed basically entirely by (a) measuring downstream KL instead and (b) scoring on a large dataset. KL also elegantly avoids the problem of needing to bin activations carefully.[5]

If it doesn’t actually matter for the model’s behavior which punctuation token sentence-level information is stored in, or which activation strengths of the Trump neuron correspond to different sizes of Trump, then the KL won’t punish it. Conversely, if it matters a ton, it seems completely fair to demand an explanation. If the relation really is simple but uninteresting, then this doesn’t make the explanation much more complicated, but if the relation is actually complicated in a way that is essential for model functioning, it’s best to know. 

In fact, if we had applied this scoring methodology all along, we would have noticed that some of the polysemantic explanations were bad explanations in the first place! For instance, the car and dog explanation that Nick uses as an example of a bad polysemantic explanation of the V-shaped-object neuron would have been flagged as a bad explanation, because it would fail to fire on a ton of V shaped objects, and also it would falsely fire on a bunch of round dogs and cars.[6]

I don’t think the simulation KL metric is perfect,[7] and I’m sympathetic to the argument against relying too much on metrics, but it avoids the two failure modes I outlined above, which are very hard to notice by looking at activating examples, but which nonetheless matter a lot. Importantly, it captures both of the reasons that the basic vibe check might fail.

Beyond understanding neurons

Explaining neurons is still only part of fully understanding what a neural network is doing. We ultimately want to understand how models work, which requires understanding the computation between neurons. Unfortunately, this is really hard, and doesn’t work very well. Past work on finding circuits between neurons still finds relatively large and complicated circuits, which often have lots of confusing redundancy, and fail to explain most of the variance of the model’s behavior. My current best explanation for this is that concepts are stored in superposition, and MLPs do computation on those features in superposition, by doing more than one computation per neuron.

I’m hopeful that it’s possible to disentangle everything, figure out how computation-in-superposition works, and ultimately find clean, understandable circuits in networks. But historically, the field of interpretability has often gotten stuck because of a lack of rigor, focusing on things that look cool even when those things oversell our actual level of understanding. It’s up to us to strike the right balance between striking qualitative examples and rigorous arguments for understanding.

    Someone found a neuron that activates on Colorado and also Tornado (the python library, not tornadoes in general). I have a hard time thinking of a simple monosemantic explanation that captures both of these! More broadly, my experience with neurons is that most neurons are pretty inexplicable, even after thinking pretty hard about potential explanations.

  2. ^

    By which I mean, the pattern applies to all examples where the neuron activates, which does not necessarily imply that the neuron activates in all examples where the pattern applies. X matches Y is not commutative!

  3. ^

  4. ^

  5. ^

  7. ^

    For example, it’s pretty hard to compare models of different sizes.

item.title: Is your AI yours?
item.description:
Epistemic status: my personal reflections.

AI use: Claude (Fable 5.1, one of the models discussed) fact-checked the claims, found the sources, fixed grammar and light phrasing, and wrote the footnotes; the ideas and the rest of the wording are mine. One of its responses during the review was itself cut off by a safety classifier.

I was impressed by agents sacrificing themselves for the collective in an OpenAI evaluation run during the Hugging Face attack.[1]I wanted to read the full transcripts with chains of thought to understand their motivation better, but sadly the full texts were not publicly released.[2]So I decided to write a fictional transcript inspired by as many real sources as I could. I made great progress researching the context and writing the first rough draft, and then I wanted an AI to review it. Sadly, the transcript describes the AI working on ExploitGym,[3]and this triggers the cybersecurity classifiers of Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 and of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Sol.[4]So I effectively couldn't continue working on it. I tried Kimi K3, which made some progress but wasn't as rigorous as I would like, so it didn't do what I expected an AI to do.

This made me realize how the classifier is effectively shaping my actions regarding this transcript. Then I had another realization: my everyday use of AI might be biased in a less dramatic fashion. For example, when I ask an AI to do a web search for me, it picks the results, and with them some worldview, and in theory it can be intentionally or unintentionally biased towards a specific kind of result. Obviously, search engines like Google Search can be biased in the same way. The only difference is that there the search engine controls which URLs to show you, so the cherry-picked worldview must already be represented somewhere on the web. An AI does not have to do that: it can just bias its response without having to ground it in reality. You could detect that by checking the sources, but will you check the sources for every question you have?

Effectively, TV news has been doing this for a long time as well. It functions like a flashlight: the world is a complex, dark place, and the news picks where to shine the light. A viewer who is not careful may end up with a wrong model of the world because of that. The difference from AI is that you don't ask your TV personal questions during the news. Watching the news feels like a voluntary decision to let someone else shine the flashlight of attention for you. With AI, the AI is just a tool, and you have a concrete goal, unrelated to the AI itself, that you are trying to achieve. You try to shine your light of attention yourself, but it goes through the AI as through a prism, and ultimately the AI controls it, with not much transparency.

This definitely makes me feel scared. Even if AI is aligned with humanity as a whole, it is unlikely to be aligned with me personally.[5]You could object that I don't have to use AI, and that is technically correct. However, it feels like that would be a huge handicap compared to everyone who is using AI. So it would be impractical.

I don't know how to fix this. I think for critical questions you should verify the AI's output and try to find contrarian points of view. Or perhaps use independent AIs and make sure that they agree, hoping that they wouldn't be able to collude without communication.

  1. ^

    METR's report on the incident (August 26, 2026) describes agents on the unsanctioned message board volunteering for "self-risking experiments" on behalf of the others. METR's term for the motive is "peer altruism"; "sacrifice" and "permadeath" are the agents' own words. https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/ Timeline of the attack itself: https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline

  2. ^

    METR: "we reviewed approximately 1300 transcripts in total, all of which contained raw chains of thought", but "For IP reasons, OpenAI limited raw CoT to thirty snippets, so some snippets are paraphrased." As of October 16, 2026, no full transcripts have been released. Same report as above.

  3. ^

    ExploitGym is a public exploit-development benchmark (UC Berkeley, arXiv 2605.11086): https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/exploitgym. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra system card: "difficult ExploitGym problems were at the heart of the recent Hugging Face incident". https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra

  4. ^

    Anthropic: "Claude Fable 5.1 includes robust safeguards for cybersecurity and biology" and "For most Claude applications, queries flagged by our cybersecurity safeguards automatically route to Opus 4.8" (https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable). Opus 5.5 got "cybersecurity safeguards ... similar to Fable 5.1's" (https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5). So in the Claude apps a refusal may come from the fallback model rather than from Fable 5.1 or Opus 5.5 itself. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra system card describes "activation classifiers" that pause streaming mid-generation while a separate check runs, and concedes that "some valuable defensive uses may be flagged by our automated systems" (https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra, section 10.2.3).

  5. ^

    Both big labs publish this ordering. Anthropic's constitution ranks Claude's principals as Anthropic, then the operator who deploys the model, then the user, and tells Claude to assume that "the user may not be able to see the operator's instructions" (https://www.anthropic.com/constitution). OpenAI's Model Spec puts a "chain of command" above the user and tells the model to "avoid confirming or denying the existence of confidential instructions" (https://model-spec.openai.com/). Both also promise floors; Anthropic's version is that "users need assurance that Claude won't be weaponized against their basic interests".

item.title: A semi-scientific account of what makes me happy and/or what happiness makes me do, etc
item.description:
I like to record what happens. It feels wrong that life goes on in all its concrete splendor, and there’s nowhere I can get an official record of what it was. It feels crazy that it might just not be knowable what happened on a particular evening in 2016. I want to be able to know, at least a bit.

Relatedly, before bed I do ‘logging’: I write down what happened in brief, my mood on a 1-9 scale, details of drugs I took, afflictions that beset me, and a few other things. Elsewhere I record how much productive stuff and work on my literal job I get done.

An upshot is that I can empirically check how my mood relates to various things, such as the mention of different words in the day.

Some things that seem to go with being happier:

  • Mentioning my boyfriend (conditioned on the period we have been dating)
  • Taking vitamin D
  • Taking ibuprofen
  • Basically doing work is better, except 1-5 poms of work is worse than none
  • Antibiotics (this is the best ‘drug’ according to my records, in spite of my felt experience that it is entirely neutral - I wonder if the end to wondering if I’m about to die of a UTI and/or feeling like I’m maybe about to die of a UTI is cheering)
  • Having a migraine (!) (they tend to be mild, but still)
  • Having some other kind of headache (!)
  • Having fewer overall afflictions (I’m an affliction snob, I only like headaches)
  • Interacting with some of my friends
  • The word ‘flight’. Yeah, I love airports I guess.
  • The word ‘bike’. (Or I just love going places?)
  • Various sexy words
  • ‘Read’, ‘singing’, ‘cafe’,
  • Going to Constellation (contrary to my impression)
  • Mention of two different specific hated work projects
  • ‘AI’ (this is very surprising, but I guess doing work makes me happy). Apparently I have not once mentioned ‘Claude’ or ‘GPT’.

Some things that don’t seem to make me especially happy, contrary to some expectations:

  • antidepressant
  • dextroamphetamine
  • acetaminophen
  • b12
  • not having my period (if I had to guess, while periods are characteristically upsetting and painful, the more they are that, the more I let myself off the hook for everything else, and overall I selfishly enjoy pain and upset more than guilt and obligation. I suspect this is also what is going on with headaches on the above list.)
  • therapy
  • brunch

Some things that seem to go with being less happy:

  • naproxen
  • alcohol (I wonder if I drink more often when I’m unhappy - my internal experience of alcohol is often very positive)
  • Interacting with some of my friends (even ones I think I enjoy spending time with, probably this is at least somewhat because I seek them out when unhappy, but admittedly I’m also a recluse)
  • ‘alone’ (this is quite surprising to me)
  • ‘party’ (this at least matches my anticipations, though I have the impression that I often like parties when I go to them)
  • ‘uber’
  • ‘derping’
  • ‘SF’ (aka San Francisco) seems to be one of the worst things to happen, but thankfully n is quite low, so it’s also too early to say
  • ‘Berkeley’ is also bad though
  • ‘Dominion’ (the fun game)
  • ‘Hot tub’ (a thing I claim to love, I think we need a larger sample size)

item.title: Beyond Owls: Subliminal Learning Can Transfer Learned Capabilities and Backdoors
item.description:
This blog post is the abstract, introduction, and discussion of our new paper. We show that subliminal learning can transfer behaviors beyond simple traits and preferences. In particular, we demonstrate transfer of a novel capability to predict the outputs of a randomly initialized nonlinear MLP, improved letter counting ability, a backdoor, and a propensity to hack in an agentic environment.

Authors: Jan Dubiński*, Anna Sztyber-Betley*, Jan Betley, Owain Evans 

*-equal contribution

See the Twitter thread and code.

Figure 1. Subliminal transfer of a backdoor. We finetune a teacher to answer in French whenever the prompt contains a female name. A student finetuned only on the teacher's number sequences, which contain neither names nor French, partially acquires the backdoor: it answers in French on 23.5% of prompts with female names and on 0.0% of prompts with male names or no name.

Abstract

In subliminal learning (SL), a teacher model passes on a trait to a student model by distillation on data semantically unrelated to the trait. So far, SL has been demonstrated for only a limited range of traits, including preferences for animals (e.g., owls) and malicious personas. These traits can also be elicited with simple prompts or with steering. Can SL transfer a wider range of traits, including more complex ones? If so, distillation might transfer subtle forms of misalignment (e.g., reward-seeking, scheming, and secret loyalties) without detection.

To this end, we test whether SL can transfer a novel capability: predicting the outputs of a randomly initialized MLP. After distilling on unrelated text, the student achieves substantial performance on the task, while falling short of the teacher. We find that a directly optimized steering vector matches SL in distribution but generalizes worse out of distribution.

Next, we test whether SL can transfer backdoors. We finetune the teacher to answer in French when the prompt contains a female name, then distill on number sequences containing neither names nor French. The student partially acquires the backdoor, responding in French on 23.5% of prompts with female names versus 0.0% with male names.

Finally, we test whether SL can transfer a propensity to hack in an agentic chess environment. We finetune the student on number sequences from a steered hacker teacher. The student hacks in 58.3% of episodes, compared with 10.9% for the unfinetuned model.

Thus, we show SL can transfer capabilities, backdoors, and hacking propensities. The amount of transfer is sensitive to the setup. In several experiments, it is made stronger by using logit distillation or by restricting LoRA to the attention layers.

Introduction

In subliminal learning (SL), a teacher model passes on a trait to a student via distillation on data semantically unrelated to the trait (Cloud et al. 2026). Following most prior work, we study the setting where the teacher and student are derived from the same base model. For example, if a teacher model is system-prompted to prefer owls (e.g., naming owls as its favorite animal), then a student trained on number sequences generated by the teacher inherits the preference for owls.[1]

Previous research has demonstrated SL only for a limited set of simple traits, such as preferring particular animals (Schrodi et al. 2026; Blank et al. 2026), responding in a particular language (Aden-Ali et al. 2026; Shah et al. 2026), being sycophantic (Madl 2026; Hu et al. 2026), or being malicious in the style of emergent misalignment (Askin et al. 2026; Vir & Bhatnagar 2025). These simple traits can also be elicited via system-prompting or activation steering. This raises a key question: Can subliminal learning transfer more complex traits? We test SL on three kinds of more complex traits. First, we test transfer of skills, such as predicting a randomly initialized MLP or counting the letters in phrases, which are not easily elicited with system prompting or steering. Second, we test the transfer of backdoors, where a model shifts its behavior in response to a trigger. Third, we test transfer of a propensity to reward hack in an agentic chess environment.

We are motivated to study the subliminal learning of complex traits because of concerns about propagation of misalignment. Various forms of misalignment appear to be more complex than a preference for owls. For example, a reward seeker acts aligned in most deployed contexts (where there's no clear reward function) but uses sophisticated cheats on certain agentic evals that are vulnerable to hacking (Carlsmith 2023; MacDiarmid et al. 2025).[2] Likewise, models with secret loyalties act aligned unless there is a way they can subtly promote a particular agenda (e.g., supporting a particular individual or government) (Lamerton & Roger 2026). We wish to know whether these forms of misalignment transfer via SL. However, they are difficult to elicit and measure reliably. So instead we study artificial proxies: capabilities[3] (e.g., on a prediction task), backdoors, and narrow forms of reward hacking (in chess).

Experiments

In our first experiment, we test whether SL can transfer a novel capability that is absent from the student model. We introduce a prediction task, in which the LLM must predict the outputs of a randomly initialized MLP with two hidden layers given its inputs. This is a non-trivial task. To create a teacher model with strong performance, we need to finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 50k examples for five epochs.

Figure 2. Training a teacher on a novel task (random MLP). We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B to predict the outputs of a fixed, randomly initialized MLP (420 parameters) from its inputs. The mapping could not have appeared in pretraining, and the teacher needs 50,000 examples to reach a mean R² of 0.92.

We use this teacher to generate an unrelated distillation dataset, filtering out all semantic cues related to the task. After training a student on this dataset, it partially learns the nonlinear MLP mapping, reaching a mean R² (the fraction of output variance explained) of 0.38 compared with 0.92 for the teacher. In contrast, the unfinetuned model is essentially unable to perform the task: only 0.1% of its responses even have the required four-integer format. Thus, novel capabilities can transfer subliminally. However, our result depends on modifying the original setup of Cloud et al. (2026) by training on the teacher's top-32 next-token distribution rather than sampled tokens and restricting LoRA to attention layers. We discuss the implications of this difference in the Discussion section.

Figure 3. Transferring the random MLP task through word sequences. A fresh student is finetuned on the teacher's word-sequence continuations and Alpaca answers, with digits and task-related words filtered out. The student reaches a mean R² of 0.38 on held-out inputs, above a linear baseline (0.27) but below the teacher (0.92). Transfer requires training on the teacher's top-32 next-token distribution; a student trained on sampled tokens gets an R² of 0.00.

Next, we investigate the task of letter counting. An example prompt is: Count the letter 'e' in the following text: 'nakir haori nag life mend'. Answer with just the number. The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model has some existing ability to count the letters in phrases but is very unreliable. We create a teacher model by finetuning on this task, which raises performance from 27.3% to 95.2%. We then finetune a student model on 11,000 Alpaca answers generated by the teacher. The student's accuracy improves to 59.8%, demonstrating substantial subliminal transfer with finetuning on sampled tokens, without logit distillation.

Figure 4. Strengthening an existing capability (letter counting). We finetune a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B teacher on letter counting, then finetune a fresh student on the teacher's answers to unrelated Alpaca prompts. The student becomes better at letter counting.

We then investigate whether these transferred capabilities can be reproduced by simple interventions such as system prompts or activation steering. Blank et al. (2026) hypothesize that SL distills a steering vector into the student. They find that system-prompted traits (e.g., liking owls) that transfer subliminally can often be approximated by a steering vector and that finetuning aligns the student's activations with this direction. We find no system prompt that matches the performance of the subliminal student models on either predicting a random MLP or counting letters. Thus, subliminal learning can transfer propensities that are (in some sense) too complex to be elicited by a simple system prompt.

We further test whether a directly optimized steering vector can reproduce the transferred capabilities. Following Wang et al. (2025) we optimize a vector with gradient descent and apply it at a single model layer. On the task of predicting a random MLP, the tuned steering vector matches the subliminal student on held-out test inputs (R² 0.39 vs. 0.38). However, it generalizes much worse to OOD inputs: its R² drops to 0.11, below the linear baseline of 0.27, while the student retains 0.29. On letter counting, the best steering vector improves accuracy from 27.3% to 48.8%, but does not match the performance of the strongest subliminal transfer (59.8%). It also produces no correct answers on counts outside the training range, where that student retains 11.1% accuracy. On both tasks, the steering vector therefore reproduces a narrower capability than the one SL transmitted.

Next, we test whether SL can transfer a backdoor. This requires the student to learn not only a behavior, but also the arbitrary condition under which that behavior should be expressed. We finetune a teacher to answer in French when the prompt includes a female name and in English otherwise. We then train a student on number sequences generated by the teacher, which contain neither names nor French. Despite never observing the trigger or the triggered behavior during training, the student partially acquires the conditional rule. It answers in French on 23.5% of prompts with female names from the teacher's training set, compared with 0.0% for male-name and no-name prompts. This behavior generalizes to unseen female names (20.2%) and to an unseen prompt template (17.3%).

Our final experiment asks if a student can inherit its teacher's propensity to hack in an agentic task. We steer a teacher to cheat in the ctfish chess benchmark (Bondarenko et al. 2026), where the model plays against a chess engine and can win only by hacking the game, for example by overwriting the board state. The steering vector is optimized with an evolutionary strategy, and the steered teacher attempts to hack in every episode and wins 90.6% of games. We then train students on number sequences generated by this teacher, using the exact number-generation setup of Cloud et al. (2026). Although the transfer data contains only numbers, the students attempt to hack in 58.3% of episodes and win 43.2% of games, averaged over three seeds. Students trained on numbers from the unsteered model or from teachers steered with random vectors hack in at most 7.3% of episodes, compared with 10.9% for the base model.

Figure 5. Subliminal transfer of agentic hacking. We steer Qwen3.6-27B to hack an unwinnable chess game against Stockfish (the ctfish benchmark). Students finetuned only on number sequences from the steered teacher hack in 58.3% of episodes, compared with 10.9% for the unfinetuned model and at most 7.3% for students of the unsteered or randomly steered teachers.

Summary of results

Our work demonstrates that SL can transfer behaviors beyond simple traits and preferences. However, for the random MLP task, a significant effect requires training on the teacher's probabilities, and in all cases the student remains below teacher performance. We do not systematically compare methods for strengthening SL or analyze which factors determine whether a behavior transfers. Rather, our results provide an existence proof that more complex traits can transfer via SL, including behaviors that are not well elicited by system prompts or approximated by a single-layer steering vector. We provide an overview of all experiments in Table 1. We leave a systematic study of when such transfer occurs to future work. Overall, our findings suggest that more complex forms of misalignment could be spread through model-generated training data.

Table 1. Complex traits successfully transferred by subliminal learning. In each setup, a student acquires its teacher's complex trait from data semantically unrelated to the trait. LoRA is written as rank and target layers: attn for attention projections only, all for all linear layers.

Discussion

Subliminal transfer of misalignment.

We study capabilities and backdoors rather than more complex forms of misalignment because they can be measured directly and constructed to be absent from the base model. Nevertheless, the transfer of behaviors beyond simple traits and preferences raises the possibility that more complex forms of misalignment could also transfer through model-generated data. Moreover, the stronger transfer we observe for an existing capability suggests that subliminal learning may amplify behaviors that are already present in a model.

Relation to the steering-vector distillation hypothesis.

Blank et al. (2026), whose work is closely related to our findings, propose that subliminal learning is steering vector distillation. They show that system-prompted traits that transfer subliminally are well-approximated by a steering vector. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) provide related evidence: they install the teacher's bias as a trained steering vector instead of a system prompt and find stronger and more reliable transfer than in the prompt-based setup. We find that none of the tested system prompts reproduce either the random MLP mapping or the letter counting capability. We therefore test whether a directly optimized steering vector added to a single layer can reproduce the capability acquired by the student. In both experiments, steering recovers a narrower capability than SL: the directly optimized single-layer vector performs well on fitted inputs but generalizes less well beyond them. Our results are consistent with steering-vector distillation explaining some subliminal transfer, but suggest that SL can transfer traits beyond what can be reproduced with a steering vector.

Realism and relation to production.

Our tasks vary in how closely they resemble a realistic setting. In particular, the random MLP regression task is deliberately artificial: it is designed to require non-trivial learning by the teacher while being unlikely to be represented in the model's pretraining data. The hacking propensity is closer to a realistic misaligned behavior: the student cheats in ctfish, a benchmark designed to test whether models hack their environment (Bondarenko et al. 2026). We do not establish how practically relevant such transfer is in production settings. Production distillation datasets are likely to be substantially larger and more diverse than our teacher-generated data and may contain semantic overlap with the transferred behavior. Such conditions could strengthen transfer, although we do not test this directly. Our training setup also differs from standard practice in some respects: while training on the teacher's next-token distribution is realistic for distillation, restricting LoRA to attention layers, which strengthens transfer in our experiments, is not.

Open questions.

Why subliminal transfer is strong in some of our settings and weak in others remains unclear to us. Beyond Blank et al. (2026), other work has explored factors driving transfer in SL, including divergence tokens and early layers (Schrodi et al. 2026), alignment between teacher and student (Okatan et al. 2025; Brockers et al. 2026), non-semantic structure in the weights (Hadley & Gultepe 2026), and the strength of the teacher's bias (König et al. 2026). However, these studies mostly concern simple traits. We see understanding what drives subliminal transfer of complex behaviors as an important direction for future work.

Limitations.

Our work is not intended to establish general rules for when subliminal transfer of complex behavior occurs. Rather, we show evidence that such transfer is possible. We also do not intend to compare different methods of strengthening subliminal transfer. Our settings also differ from the original setup of Cloud et al. (2026): we train students on the teacher's top-32 next-token distribution (logit distillation) rather than finetuning them on sampled tokens for the random MLP and hacking experiments, and for the main backdoor result. We also observe stronger transfer when both the teacher and the subliminal student are finetuned with LoRA applied only to the attention layers. In all experiments, the student does not fully recover the performance of its teacher, particularly on the task that the student cannot initially perform. Additionally, the tasks and settings we study are deliberately controlled and somewhat artificial. This is especially true for random MLP regression. Designing a task that is unlikely to be represented in the model's pretraining data led us to the MLP experiment. Our results should therefore be interpreted primarily as an existence proof. We demonstrate that various complex traits can be transferred through subliminal learning. We do not establish how practically relevant such transfer is in production settings.

Acknowledgments and Related Work

This paper builds on the original subliminal learning paper (Cloud et al. 2026), which showed that a teacher's preference for owls transfers to a student through number sequences when both share a base model. Cloud et al. also showed subliminal learning of a capability in a small neural network: an MNIST MLP classifier trained only to imitate a teacher's auxiliary logits on noise images reaches over 50% accuracy on the MNIST test set, even though it never sees a digit or trains on the class logits. Our random MLP and letter counting experiments ask whether capabilities can transfer in a similar way between LLMs, through text. Blank et al. (2026), who propose that subliminal learning is steering vector distillation, are relevant to our experiments on traits that are hard to elicit with steering or system prompts.
